title: Optimize Quality Guardrails (Gating) — Exec One-Pager
content:
Redwood Inference — Optimize Quality Guardrails (Gating)
Exec One-Pager (v0.6)

Owner: Priya Natarajan (Exec Sponsor)
DRI: Aditya Rao (Product, Optimize)
Core partners: Applied ML/Evals (Jonas Weber, Selene Huang, Sana Farid), Control Plane/Policy (Ethan Park, Jordan Lee), SRE (Sean Gallagher)

1) Summary (what we’re doing)
We are introducing mandatory “quality guardrails” that gate any Optimize-driven configuration change (batching, caching, quantization profile changes, routing tweaks) behind evaluation checks and regression thresholds.

Practically: when a user clicks “Apply Optimize Recommendation” (Console or API), the control plane will (a) run or fetch a relevant eval suite against the current vs proposed configuration, (b) compare results to a versioned threshold policy, and (c) allow/deny the apply with clear pass/fail reasons, artifact links, and an audited override path.

Why this matters: Optimize can deliver meaningful cost savings, but config changes can materially impact response quality. This project converts quality protection from “best effort” to a standardized, auditable enforcement mechanism.

2) Why now (timing + triggers)
We’re seeing increasing overlap of:
- Higher adoption of Optimize in production (more applies per week, more automated workflows).
- Larger performance levers being used (especially quantization + aggressive batching) that have non-trivial quality risk.
- More enterprise scrutiny (auditability, change control, “prove checks ran before you changed anything”).

Specific triggers:
- Customer escalation: quality regression after quantization apply (Jira SUP-18422). The incident was recoverable, but it exposed the gap: we had tooling to measure regressions, not a mandatory gate to prevent them.
- Enterprise requests for audit logs that show: who applied what, which evals ran, results, and whether an override occurred (Jira SUP-18544).
- Internal pilot learnings: even when teams “intend” to run evals, execution becomes inconsistent under delivery pressure. We need productized guardrails.

3) Customer impact (who benefits + what changes)
Primary beneficiaries:
- Enterprise and regulated customers (Dedicated/Private): reduction in production quality regressions, improved trust in Optimize and in Redwood operational rigor.
- Mid-market SaaS: safer self-serve adoption, fewer support escalations after cost optimizations.
- Internal: clearer accountability and faster triage when something fails (eval artifacts + standardized failure reasons).

User-visible behavior changes:
- “Apply” may be blocked if quality gates fail or the eval runner is unavailable (depending on tenant tier / policy).
- Users will see: which metrics regressed, by how much, confidence signals, and links to prompt set + suite revisions.
- A controlled override path exists for restricted roles (with justification + full audit logging). Default intent is that overrides are rare and measurable.

4) Business impact (economics + trust)
This is a trust and reliability investment that preserves Optimize revenue expansion:
- Protects retention / expansion: fewer regressions → fewer churn triggers and fewer “turn Optimize off” outcomes.
- Improves enterprise close rates: auditable gating + change control aligns with procurement/security requirements.
- Preserves cost-savings narrative: we can confidently recommend larger optimizations when we can prove quality constraints.

5) Cost vs quality tradeoffs (how we avoid over-blocking)
Key tension: aggressive gating can create false positives (blocking safe changes), slowing adoption and reducing savings.

Our approach:
- Tiered enforcement with feature flags:
  1) Observe-only (log decisions, do not block)
  2) Soft-block (block by default, allow override where allowed)
  3) Hard-block (no override except break-glass policy)
- Thresholds are versioned and scoped (per model family + workload type + optimization type) to reduce “one-size-fits-all” error.
- Statistical guardrails: minimum sample sizes and confidence interval rules where rubric graders are noisy (vs only fixed deltas).
- Cache eval results keyed by model version + prompt-set revision + suite + config delta to keep marginal latency/cost low.
- Clear failure reasons: distinguish “true regression” vs “insufficient evidence” vs “runner timeout” to avoid blocking for non-quality reasons.

Expected incremental compute cost:
- Initial pilot will increase eval traffic, but caching and suite selection reduce repeat runs.
- We will cap concurrency and isolate eval traffic from customer serving traffic (SRE + Runtime constraints) to avoid creating platform risk.

6) What “good” looks like (success metrics)
Product / customer outcomes:
- Material reduction in customer-visible quality regressions attributable to Optimize applies (target: down significantly quarter-over-quarter; exact KPI tracked in Guardrails KPI sheet).
- Decrease in “Optimize caused quality regression” support escalations.
- Increased enterprise confidence: audit log completeness + export readiness.

Operational outcomes:
- Gating decision latency within acceptable bounds for apply flow (with async workflow + UI status states).
- Eval runner reliability (backlog/timeout rates within SRE thresholds).
- Override rate remains low and declines over time as thresholds + prompt sets mature.

7) Key risks + mitigations
Risk A: False positives block safe savings (adoption friction)
- Mitigation: staged rollout, observe-only baseline, calibrate thresholds with historical runs (backfill), and per-workload thresholding.

Risk B: False negatives allow regressions (trust failure)
- Mitigation: expand prompt set coverage for high-risk surfaces (tool-calling, structured output, formatting-sensitive use cases), add quantization-specific suites, and post-apply monitoring correlation.

Risk C: Eval runner reliability / timeouts degrade apply experience
- Mitigation: async job runner with strict SLAs, caching, retries, and explicit safe-degrade policy by tier; SRE dashboards + alerting; operational tooling to replay runs.

Risk D: Metric gaming / misaligned proxies
- Mitigation: metric taxonomy and ownership in Applied ML; require suite versioning and prompt-set revision pinning; periodic reviews (threshold tuning cadence).

Risk E: Governance concerns around overrides (“rubber stamp”)
- Mitigation: RBAC restrictions, optional second-approver for selected enterprise tiers, rate limits, justification required, and executive visibility into override volume and reasons.

Risk F: Compliance and data handling
- Mitigation: audit events are PII-safe, payload redaction rules, artifact retention policy (summaries vs raw outputs), and alignment with Security/Compliance review.

8) Timeline to default-on (expected)
Phases (current plan):
- Phase 0 — Discovery (2–3 weeks)
  - Finalize metric taxonomy + initial threshold policy draft
  - Prompt set coverage targets (minimum viable per workload type)
  - Confirm enforcement design + failure modes

- Phase 1 — Build (4–6 weeks)
  - Threshold schema + policy engine integration
  - Eval runner integration (async + caching)
  - Console + API gating plumbing and UI states
  - Audit logging + initial dashboards

- Phase 2 — Pilot (3–4 weeks)
  - Internal canary + small set of design partners
  - Tune thresholds, fix reliability issues, reduce false positives
  - Validate override path + audit log exports

- Phase 3 — GA / Default-on (2–4 weeks)
  - Roll out by tenant tier (hosted → dedicated → private, per policy)
  - Move from soft-block to hard-block for most optimization types
  - Publish customer-facing docs and support playbooks

Net: ~11–17 weeks from kickoff to default-on gating for Optimize applies, assuming no major reliability surprises.

9) Decisions needed / executive asks
1) Policy stance on overrides:
- Proposed default: Overrides allowed only for restricted roles on higher tiers, with justification + full audit logging; some tenants may opt into “no overrides”.
- Decision needed: Should any tier require 2-person approval (maker-checker) by default, or only as an enterprise add-on?

2) Safe-degrade behavior when eval runner is down:
- Proposed: block applies for most tiers (quality-first) and allow a “manual approval” path only where contractually required and auditable.
- Decision needed: confirm quality-first default vs uptime-first default for Dedicated/Private.

3) Resourcing commitment for prompt sets + threshold tuning:
- Guardrails are only as good as coverage + calibration.
- Ask: commit ongoing Applied ML + Product cycles (post-GA) for prompt set maintenance and quarterly threshold review.

10) Notes / references (for follow-up)
- ADRs: enforcement point (control plane), threshold schema + versioning
- Customer signals: SUP-18422 (quality regression after quant apply), SUP-18544 (audit log evidence request)
- Tracking: Linear PM-842 initiative + ENG build tickets

Appendix (1-liners)
- What’s new: “Quality checks become a gate, not a recommendation.”
- What’s the unlock: More aggressive cost savings with confidence + enterprise-grade auditability.
- What can go wrong: Over-blocking due to noisy evals, or under-blocking due to insufficient coverage. Both are addressed via phased rollout + ongoing tuning.
